finding.summary: Hand-rolled SQL literal escaping reinvents `mysql2`'s own escaper, which is already imported in this file
finding.evidence: `import * as mysql from 'mysql2/promise'` is already present (line 3), and mysql2 re-exports SqlString's `escape`/`format` (also available as `pool.escape()`). The delta grows a bespoke `sql()` helper (`value.replace(/\\/g,'\\\\').replace(/'/g,"''")`) plus a paragraph of dialect commentary and dedicated unit tests to re-derive escaping rules the dependency already implements correctly and completely (it also handles \0, \n, \r, \x1a and "). The repo's stated norm is reuse over re-implementation; the fact that this round had to add a backslash case after shipping a quote-only version is exactly the maintenance cost that reuse avoids. `mysql.escape(value)` (or `mysql.format('… document_id = ?', [id])` for the whole predicate) gives the same string-interpolation-without-prepared-statements approach the design doc prescribes, with no bespoke escaper to keep in sync.

verdict.reason: The finding asserts a bespoke SQL escaper (`value.replace(/\\/g,'\\\\').replace(/'/g,"''")`) duplicating mysql2's escaper. That code is not present. `analytics-warehouse.service.ts:42-44` defines `function sql(value: string) { return mysql.escape(value); }` — it already delegates to mysql2's `escape`, exactly the remedy the finding prescribes. The comment block at lines 32-41 states the delegation rationale and explains the thin wrapper (mysql2's `escape` second arg is `stringifyObjects`, which `documentIds.map(sql)` at line 158 would otherwise fill with the array index) — it is not a re-derivation of escaping rules. The tests likewise do not re-derive rules: spec lines 73-89 and 102 build expectations by calling `mysql.escape(...)` and only assert that the builders route ids through it. A repo-wide grep for the quoted replace patterns yields no hits in backend/analytics (only unrelated font/XML escapers and an archived task doc). No duplication of an existing module remains.
